# Deriving F = ma From the Rate of Change of Momentum

<!-- STEP id="newtons-actual-statement" -->
Newton's second law, in its original form: **the rate of change of an object's momentum is directly proportional to the net force applied to it, and happens in the direction of that force.**

<!-- STEP id="rate-of-change" -->
"Rate of change" means "how much, per second" — divide the change in momentum by the time it took:

$$\frac{\Delta p}{t} = \frac{m(v-u)}{t}$$

<!-- STEP id="recognize-acceleration" -->
But $\frac{v-u}{t}$ is exactly the definition of acceleration, a. So the rate of change of momentum is simply:

$$\frac{\Delta p}{t} = ma$$

<!-- STEP id="proportional-to-force" -->
Net force is proportional to that rate of change:

$$F \propto ma$$

A proportionality needs a constant to become an equation: $F = kma$.

<!-- STEP id="choosing-the-unit" -->
We define the **newton**, the unit of force, as exactly the force that gives a 1 kg object an acceleration of 1 m s⁻². That choice is what makes k = 1.

<!-- STEP id="the-result" -->
$$F = ma$$

The same equation the cart-and-coins experiment found by trial — now derived algebraically, straight from how momentum changes.
